To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of thyroid autoimmunization in the offspring of type 1 diabetic patients is increased, that thyroid peroxidase antibodies are often the last auto-antibodies to appear and that thyroid autoimmunity is most common in girls and in children who have multiple first-degree relatives with type 1 diabetic and who have antibodies to GAD.
thyroid autoantibody appearance was frequent in children at risk for type 1 diabetes and was most frequent in girls and in children who had a family history of type 1 diabetes or islet antibodies.
thyroid autoimmunity is frequent and appears late in childhood and adolescence in children at risk for type 1 diabetes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of factors that contribute to the pathogenesis of autoimmune diabetes in children.
the study of the pathogenesis, natural course and treatment of autoimmune diseases.
the study of the genetic and environmental determinants of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the risk for thyroid autoimmunity is increased in children with type 1diabetes and that the risk is highest during the late childhood and adolescence, but it does not necessarily mean that thyroid autoimmunity in these children will progress to clinical thyroid dysfunction, and that the thyroid dysfunction is not necessarily related to the type 1 diabetes mellitus.
thyroid autoimmunity is frequent and not synchronous to the other autoantibody appearance in at-risk children.

the risk for thyroid autoimmunity is increased in children with multiple first-degree relatives with type 1A diabetes, in girls and in children with other forms of autoantibodies, but that it is not synchronous to other autoimmune disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
thyroid autoimmunity is frequent in children at risk of developing type 1 diabetes and the risk increases in late childhood.
thyroid autoimmunity is a frequent complication of type 1 and type 2 diabetes and can be detected in a high percentage of diabetic patients, but it is not a prerequisite for diabetes development.

thyroid autoimmunity is frequent in children of patients with Type 1 diabetes, that it is often the last autoimmunity to appear in those who have other autoantibody, and that it is often found in children with a family history of Type 1 diabetes and/or other autoimmune diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
thyroid autoantibody appearance is frequent and is often the last auto-antibody to appear in children of patients with diabetes who have other autoantibody markers of autoimmune disease.
thyroid autoantibody positivity in childhood is common and is associated with multiple autoimmunity and female gender.
the appearance of thyroid peroxidase autoantibodies can be used as a marker for endocrine autoimmunity.
